title: LSASS memory opened with full-access masks by attacker PowerShell session (pbeesly) on scranton and nashua
summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16 (UTC) the user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local requested handles to \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe from powershell.exe with AccessMask 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (DELETE, WRITE_DAC, WRITE_OWNER, VM operation, read/write process memory, duplicate handle, create thread). Sysmon corroborates the same opens from PowerShell.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 03:05:16.623/03:05:16.654. At 03:09:29 the same user, via a remote PowerShell session (wsmprovhost.exe, logon 0x85AAD2) on nashua.dmevals.local, again opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff. This occurred inside a hands-on-keyboard intrusion: the same pbeesly session had just run a PowerShell toolkit (readme.ps1 / psversion.ps1 from C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite) containing Keystroke-Check, Get-Keystrokes, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Get-Clipboard, Get-PrivateKeys and Invoke-Exfil, and had executed accesschk.exe. No lsass.dmp file was written to disk in the observed window, but the access masks are those of a memory-read/credential-dump attempt against LSASS. Other LSASS opens in the dataset (svchost.exe 0x1000/0x1400, CollectGuestLogs.exe, MsMpEng.exe, AntimalwareConfig.exe, wininit/csrss at process start) are normal system behaviour.

title: SAM database and SAM_DOMAIN/SAM_SERVER handles opened by lsass.exe on scranton (system-account context, no attacker tooling)
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01T23:19:10-23:19:22 (local, = 03:19 UTC) lsass.exe running as SCRANTON$ (S-1-5-18, logon 0x3E7) requested handles to SAM_SERVER 'SAM' (0xf003f), SAM_DOMAIN 'SCRANTON' (0xf07df) and SAM_ALIAS 'DOMAINS\Builtin\Aliases\00000221' (0xf), and wrote HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F. This is the local LSA/SAM service itself, not an external dumping tool: no reg save of HKLM\SAM/SECURITY, no esentutl/ntdsutil, and no SAM/SECURITY hive file copies were found (the only file-create hits matching SAM/SECURITY were Prefetch .pf files). The SAM access coincides with an lsass.exe restart on the host (lsass.exe process create at 03:19:09.809, LsaPid write 0x2ec, CredentialGuard Enabled=0), i.e. normal LSA initialization. No evidence of an adversary extracting local account hashes.

title: HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 writes by lsass.exe on nashua — normal cached-credential maintenance, not dumping
summary: On nashua.dmevals.local, lsass.exe (PID 728) set the value HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 to 'Binary Data' at 03:11:40, 03:12:46, 03:13:49 and 03:15:03 on 2020-05-02. These are writes by the LSA process itself to the cached-domain-credential cache, consistent with normal logon/cache updates (the same host was being accessed by pbeesly around this time), not an external read of the cache. No security-audit handle events on SECURITY\Cache objects and no PowerShell referencing mscache/DCC2 were found, so there is no evidence of cached credential extraction.

title: No NTDS.dit / volume-shadow / ntdsutil activity observed
summary: Searches for NTDS file creation, ntdsutil/vssadmin/diskshadow command lines in Sysmon and Security 4688, and for shadow/VSS/ntds strings in windows.other and PowerShell script blocks returned no hits. The only domain-controller-like host in scope (newyork) shows only routine service activity (UsoClient, dsregcmd, W32Time). No evidence of NTDS extraction.

title: No LSA Secrets / SECURITY hive dumping observed
summary: No process creations with secrets/lsadump/reg save HKLM\SECURITY, no 4656/4663/4670 events on SECURITY Policy Secrets objects, and no PowerShell or windows.other messages referencing LSA secrets were found. The only SECURITY-related registry activity was lsass.exe writing HKLM\SECURITY\Cache\NL$1 on nashua (see T1003.005).

title: No DCSync / DRSUAPI replication abuse observed
summary: No process command lines containing drsuapi/lsadump/dcsync and no PowerShell script blocks referencing DCSync/lsadump/drsuapi were found. The attacker's PowerShell activity on scranton/nashua focused on keystroke logging, screen capture, clipboard, private-key export and exfiltration, plus PsExec to NASHUA with plaintext credentials, but no directory replication request was observed in the available telemetry.

title: Azure Network Watcher agent performs netsh packet capture on SCRANTON (platform telemetry, not adversary sniffing)
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:19:17Z, netsh.exe was launched as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM (LogonId 0x3e7, session 0) with 'trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-DFE6-43C7-8FA8-8D3AC5AA8726\B91E06C5-1C7C-4830-9A76-74FA211560A7.etl"' and stopped at 03:19:24Z with 'netsh trace stop'. The parent is the Microsoft Azure NetworkWatcherAgent service (C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe /service), which was itself installed/started as a service on the same host minutes earlier (4688 'Install /service /autoStart', 'Test /service /autoStart', '/service'). This is the Azure platform's own packet-capture capability, not attacker-driven sniffing: no pcap/npcap/winpcap driver load, no tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap execution, and no sniff/promiscuous command lines were found anywhere in the Windows telemetry.

title: No adversary network-sniffing tooling observed; the real intrusion on NASHUA used a PyInstaller python.exe beacon, not a sniffer
summary: Hunting for T1040-specific artifacts across windows.sysmon, windows.security and windows.powershell returned nothing: no tcpdump/windump/wireshark/rawcap process creation, no pcap/npcap/winpcap image loads (sysmon event 6 aggregation on win.Image returned 0 buckets), no sniff/promisc/pcap command lines, and no capture-driver service installs (the only 7045 services were a Java support service and PSEXESVC). The genuine compromise in this window is separate from sniffing: on scranton.dmevals.local user pbeesly ran a hidden, encoded PowerShell stager (monkey.png bitmap decode + IEX), then 'Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA' and repeated PsExec64 with plaintext credentials (\\NASHUA -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe), which spawned PSEXESVC and C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local (SHA256 43782EC4337D8F3DDB7EA0C451B3BC4F212F84C8D5571BD0A842001C859A02AE) that unpacked a PyInstaller bundle to _MEI29522 and opened many TCP connections to 192.168.0.4:8443. That is C2/lateral movement, not passive network sniffing, so T1040 is not supported by the evidence.

title: Steganography-launched hidden PowerShell opened LSASS with full access on scranton (credential API hooking / memory access)
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local a malicious screen saver C:\ProgramData\victim\â€®cod.3aka3.scr (PID 8524) wrote C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png at 02:57:00Z. At 02:58:44Z a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell (PID 2976, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, High integrity, parent control.exe /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter) was spawned that read the bitmap pixel data and IEX'd the decoded bytes (steganographic payload delivery). That same process entity {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400} then requested handles to lsass.exe (PID 736) at 03:05:16Z with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF — full-process access including PROCESS_VM_READ, the access pattern used to read credential material from LSASS memory. The call trace ends in UNKNOWN modules, not a signed security product. This is the only PowerShell-sourced full-access LSASS open in the whole dataset (all other LSASS opens are svchost 0x1000, Azure antimalware/telemetry 0x1400, or OS processes).

title: LSASS handle requests and SAM object access on scranton/nashua are OS-internal or benign PowerShell cmdlet activity
summary: The 4656 handle-request hits to lsass.exe/SAM are dominated by legitimate system activity: lsass.exe itself opening SAM_SERVER (AccessMask 0xf003f, subject SCRANTON$ logon 0x3E7), Windows Defender MsMpEng.exe, Azure CollectGuestLogs.exe, and svchost.exe. The one non-OS LSASS open outside scranton's malicious PowerShell was wsmprovhost.exe on nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29Z with 0x1F3FFF, but its call trace runs through System.ni.dll and Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll and coincides with the benign script block 'Get-Process -IncludeUserName | Select-Object UserName,SessionId' at 03:09:28-29Z, i.e. a PowerShell cmdlet enumerating process owners rather than credential theft. The remaining LSASS opens (svchost 0x1000 x286, AntimalwareConfig.exe/WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe 0x1400) are standard.

title: No MFA interception artifacts; credential access observed is LSASS memory access (T1003.001), not MFA token theft

The 4648 explicit-credential logons (15 total) are dominated by the compromised account pbeesly (9 events) used by PSEXESVC.exe on nashua.dmevals.local and by svchost.exe on scranton.dmevals.local, plus routine DWM-/UMFD-/machine-account logons from winlogon.exe/wininit.exe/taskhostw.exe. The 'Credential' registry hits (11 Sysmon 13 events) are all Windows servicing noise: lsass.exe setting DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled to 0x00000000 and services.exe creating the CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc_13619b service plus MuiCache entries. windows.other shows only 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' (event 14) and an unrelated DNS PTR registration failure. No smart-card, token, OTP, or MFA-provider interception activity was found. The genuine credential-access activity in this window is LSASS memory access: on nashua.dmevals.local wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, WinRM remote shell) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and a PowerShell/System.ni.dll call trace at 2020-05-02T03:09:29Z, and on scranton.dmevals.local powershell.exe (PID 3876) accessed lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1000 at 03:01:03Z. title: WebDAV forced authentication from scranton (10.0.1.4) to attacker-style WebDAV server 192.168.0.4, followed by SMB/ADMIN$ credential use against nashua and newyork
summary: On 2020-04-30 between 00:32:14 and 00:32:21 UTC, host 10.0.1.4 (scranton.dmevals.local, per the zeek-scranton log source) first probed 192.168.0.4 on TCP 445 and 139 (all connections REJ, i.e. SMB blocked), then immediately pivoted to HTTP/80 WebDAV against the same host. The client used the Windows WebDAV redirector user agents 'DavClnt' and 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362' and issued OPTIONS, PROPFIND, PROPPATCH, PUT, LOCK and UNLOCK against /webdav and /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z. The server repeatedly answered 401 Unauthorized and the client re-sent the requests, which is the classic forced-authentication/NTLM-coercion pattern: the victim is made to authenticate to an attacker-controlled WebDAV endpoint so its Net-NTLM hash can be captured. The same host then wrote a file to the remote WebDAV share (PUT /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z returned 201 Created, then 204 No Content, with a 2.1 MB upload on the port-80 connection), consistent with staging data to the attacker's server. In the Windows telemetry window (2020-05-02 02:55-03:28 UTC, non-overlapping with zeek) the same source address 10.0.1.4 is seen authenticating as user 'pbeesly' and as machine account 'SCRANTON$' to SYSVOL, IPC$ and ADMIN$ shares on newyork.dmevals.local and nashua.dmevals.local (9 ADMIN$ accesses to \\*\ADMIN$ -> \??\C:\windows on nashua between 23:10 and 23:18 local time), i.e. the coerced/obtained credentials were used for lateral SMB access. The SMB connections observed in Sysmon to 10.0.0.4 and 10.0.1.6 are System-process (port 445/139) domain traffic and are not themselves coercive, but the WebDAV sequence is a clear forced-authentication attempt.

title: Routine domain SMB/SYSVOL/IPC$ share access and System-process SMB connections are benign background activity
summary: The bulk of the T1187 check hits are normal domain operations, not forced authentication. Of 163 share-access events (5140/5145), the shares are only \\*\SYSVOL (69), \\*\IPC$ (65) and \\*\ADMIN$ (29) - standard Group Policy replication and remote-management shares. Many are machine-account authentications (NEWYORK$, SCRANTON$) over IPv6 link-local fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 or from 10.0.1.4, matching DFSR/GPO traffic. The 66 Sysmon event.code 3 hits on ports 445/139 all come from process.executable 'System' (PID 4) to 10.0.0.4, 10.0.1.6 and the local link-local address, i.e. kernel SMB client/server traffic, not a user-mode coercer. The 1649 Sysmon file-creation events are dominated by prefetch, EventLog lastalive*.dat, DFSR replica XML, GroupPolicy DataStore and Cortana cache files - no .lnk/.scf/.url/.library-ms coercion files were observed. Zeek SMB connections (45 to 445, 5 to 139) are internal host-to-host traffic. The PowerShell (4104) and windows.other checks for 445/WebDAV/NTLM returned zero hits. Only the 10.0.1.4 -> 192.168.0.4 WebDAV sequence is anomalous; the remaining share and SMB activity is consistent with normal AD administration.

title: Hidden PowerShell stager (control.exe parent) opened lsass with full-access 0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF on scranton
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PID 2976 (C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe, user DMEVALS\pbeesly, IntegrityLevel High) was spawned at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z by C:\Windows\System32\control.exe with the command line "PowerShell.exe" -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden -c "sal a New-Object;Add-Type -AssemblyName 'System.Drawing'; $g=a System.Drawing.Bitmap('C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png');...IEX([System.Text.Encoding]::ASCII.GetString($o[0..3932]))" — a steganographic, hidden-window, execution-policy-bypass loader. At 03:05:16Z that same process (SourceProcessGUID {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) twice with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF, i.e. PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS-equivalent rights that permit reading credential material. The call trace ends in UNKNOWN(000001996D28200D), not a Windows LSA module, indicating code injected/allocated in the PowerShell process rather than a legitimate LSA API path. This is the only PowerShell-to-lsass full-access pair in the dataset and is consistent with in-memory credential theft from lsass.

title: WMI remote-exec host (wsmprovhost.exe, user pbeesly) opened lsass with 0x1F3FFF on nashua
summary: On nashua.dmevals.local, PID 7720 (C:\windows\system32\wsmprovhost.exe -Embedding, parent svchost.exe -k DcomLaunch -p, running as DMEVALS\pbeesly) was created at 2020-05-02T03:09:23Z and six seconds later, at 03:09:29Z, opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF. The call trace runs through System.ni.dll and Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, showing the access was made from PowerShell code executed inside a WMI/WinRM remote-execution host — i.e. the same operator (pbeesly) who ran the hidden stager on scranton reached nashua remotely and requested near-full access to lsass. This is the only wsmprovhost-to-lsass access in the dataset.

title: Remaining lsass process-access events are legitimate Windows LSA/AV/telemetry behaviour
summary: Of 326 Sysmon event-10 accesses to lsass.exe, 289 come from svchost.exe and the rest from AntimalwareConfig.exe (15), WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe (13), wininit.exe (2), csrss.exe (1) and services.exe (1) — normal LSA, AV and Azure guest-agent activity. The rare masks are also benign: the svchost 0x101001 access on scranton at 03:18:34Z has a call trace entirely through c:\windows\system32\lsm.dll (the LSA policy provider), and the wininit/csrss 0x1FFFFF/0x1000000 accesses at 03:19:09Z are the standard boot-time lsass initialisation by its parent processes. The two PowerShell 0x1000 accesses (read-only, VM_READ) are not credential-dumping rights. No exploit artefacts were found in windows.other (no 'exploit' messages) or in PowerShell script blocks (no Invoke-*/Exploit matches), and the Zeek notices/weirds are from a non-overlapping 2020-04-30 window with no credential-access content.

On scranton.dmevals.local, in the same session where user pbeesly ran a hidden, encoded PowerShell stager (monkey.png bitmap-decoded IEX launched from control.exe at 02:58:44), a PowerShell.exe process (PID 2976) opened the Microsoft Edge browser process (PID 7748, C:\Windows\SystemApps\Microsoft.MicrosoftEdge_8wekyb3d8bbwe\MicrosoftEdge.exe) with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF at 2020-05-02T03:05:17Z, and immediately afterwards opened MicrosoftEdgeSH.exe and MicrosoftEdgeCP.exe with the same full access. Full-process access to a browser is the prerequisite for reading session cookies out of browser memory. No cookie file access, cookie-named command line, or cookie-related script block was observed, so the theft itself is not proven; the surrounding activity (hidden encoded PowerShell, credential-file harvesting script, PsExec, sdelete) makes this access suspicious rather than benign.

accesschk.exe run by pbeesly on SCRANTON creates 'passwordsDB' and queries the LSA registry key
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:04:34Z user pbeesly launched C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\accessChk.exe from a PowerShell parent (4688 + Sysmon 1). One second later (03:04:35Z) that process created the file C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\passwordsDB (Sysmon 11), and at 03:04:54Z it opened \REGISTRY\MACHINE\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\Lsa with AccessMask 0x1 / 'Query key value' (4656 and 4663, SubjectUserName pbeesly). This is credential reconnaissance/collection on the host: a Sysinternals access-enumeration tool being used to probe the LSA secrets key and to write a file named for passwords. It is part of a broader intrusion chain on the same host (sdelete64 wiping C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr, Draft.Zip and SysinternalsSuite.zip, then PsExec64 to NASHUA with a plaintext password).

title: Plaintext password used on PsExec64 command line to reach NASHUA, then Rar.exe archives data with a hardcoded password
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, pbeesly's PowerShell ran PsExec64.exe four times (03:11:18, 03:12:25, 03:13:28, 03:14:42Z) with the credential supplied in cleartext on the command line: -u dmevals\pbeesly -p Fl0nk3rt0n!T0by -i 2 C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe. The same string appears in PowerShell 4104 script blocks. Each attempt produced a 4648 explicit-credential logon on nashua.dmevals.local with Process Name C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe and TargetUserName pbeesly, and C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe then executed on NASHUA under PSEXESVC.exe. On NASHUA at 03:16:19Z Rar.exe was run as 'a -hpfGzq5yKw C:\Users\pbeesly\Desktop\working.zip C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\working.zip', i.e. staging collected data into a password-protected archive, after which sdelete64.exe was used to wipe Rar.exe and the zips. Credentials embedded in command lines/scripts were used to move laterally and to protect exfiltrated data.

title: Registry Password/Credential value sets are Windows service and identity-provider noise
summary: The 17 Sysmon 13 hits on registry paths containing Password/Credential are all written by legitimate system processes: svchost.exe setting HKU\.DEFAULT\Software\Microsoft\IdentityCRL\ProviderPasswordLength / ProviderPasswordCharacterGroups on nashua and scranton, lsass.exe setting DeviceGuard\Scenarios\CredentialGuard\Enabled to 0 on scranton, services.exe creating the CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc_13619b service values, and winlogon.exe writing PasswordExpiryNotification\NotShownTime. None of these are credential harvesting; the only genuine registry credential access observed is accesschk.exe reading the LSA key, reported under T1552.

title: SYSVOL GptTmpl.inf / gpt.ini reads are routine Group Policy processing, not GPP credential harvesting
summary: Zeek smb_files shows two hosts (simplerockbuild.simplerock.lan 10.0.1.4 at 2020-04-30T00:12:01Z and bobs.bigwheel.local 10.0.1.6 at 00:20:49Z) opening \\NEWYORK.dmevals.local\sysvol paths gpt.ini, Machine\Microsoft\Windows NT\SecEdit\GptTmpl.inf and the policy folder tree. These are the standard files a domain member reads during Group Policy refresh; no Groups.xml, Services.xml or ScheduledTasks.xml with cpassword was accessed, and the zeek window (2020-04-30) does not overlap the Windows host telemetry (2020-05-02). No GPP-embedded credential access is evidenced.

title: PowerShell and WinRM host processes opened LSASS with near-full access rights on scranton and nashua (pbeesly)
summary: On 2020-05-02, user pbeesly's PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff at 03:05:16.623Z and 0x1fffff at 03:05:16.654Z, with a call trace ending in an UNKNOWN module (ntdll!NtOpenProcess -> KERNELBASE -> UNKNOWN), i.e. not a normal Windows component. summary: Stacking all 326 Sysmon EID 10 events targeting lsass.exe shows the bulk is routine: svchost.exe 0x1000 (286 events), Microsoft Azure IaaSAntimalware AntimalwareConfig.exe 0x1400 (13), WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe 0x1400 (11), svchost 0x101001 (2, lsm.dll call trace), svchost 0x3000 (1, sysmain.dll), and boot-time wininit/csrss 0x1fffff/0x1000000. Security object-access auditing on lsass.exe likewise shows only CollectGuestLogs.exe (0x1410/0x10), MsMpEng.exe (0x1fffff/0x10) and lsass itself (0x1478). No vaultcmd, cmdkey, DPAPI, Credential Manager registry/file access, or 4688/4104 command lines referencing vault or credentials were found; the only 'Credential' message is a routine Credential Guard configuration event (0x0) on scranton. The two anomalous PowerShell/wsmprovhost LSASS handles are reported under T1555.

title: LSASS handle access on all four hosts is dominated by svchost.exe with benign access masks; no authentication-process modification observed
summary: 326 Sysmon event.code 10 accesses to lsass.exe were recorded between 2020-05-02T02:56 and 03:28. Stacking by source image gives svchost.exe 289 (scranton 219, newyork 30, nashua 28, utica 12), AntimalwareConfig.exe 15, WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe 13, PowerShell.exe/powershell.exe 4, wininit.exe 2, csrss.exe 1, services.exe 1, wsmprovhost.exe 1. The only PowerShell full-access handle (0x1fffff, 0x1f3fff at 03:05:16 on scranton, PID 2976) has an UNKNOWN call trace, but the surrounding PowerShell 4104/4103 records for that window show only screen-capture code (Invoke-ScreenCapture, Add-Type System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing, Start-Job 'Screenshot'), not credential access. No 4657 registry write to LSA/SAM/cryptdll/msv1_0, no 4688 command line referencing lsass/cryptdll/msv1_0, and no PowerShell script block referencing lsass/cryptdll/msv1_0 was found.

title: Network logons are machine-account and PsExec traffic; no DC authentication backdoor
summary: 218 type-3 logons (4624) are dominated by the NEWYORK$ machine account from ::1, fe80::e40c:95b6:b0a7:6429 and 10.0.0.4 on newyork.dmevals.local, i.e. normal machine-account network authentication. No 4657 write to LSA/SAM/cryptdll/msv1_0 and no lsass/cryptdll reference in windows.other or PowerShell script blocks was found.

summary: No 4657 registry write to Notification Packages/Password/lsass, no 4688 command line containing Notification or PasswordFilter, no PowerShell script block containing Notification/PasswordFilter/lsass, and no Sysmon event.code 11 file creation of a .dll under System32 were returned. The only service installs in windows.other are PSEXESVC (%SystemRoot%\PSEXESVC.exe, demand start, four times on nashua.dmevals.local by pbeesly) and 'Java(TM) Virtual Machine Support Service' (C:\Windows\System32\javamtsup.exe, auto start, on scranton.dmevals.local) — neither is a password filter package.

title: No MFA/authentication-policy registry or directory changes
summary: No 4739, no 5136 and no 4738 events were returned in windows.security or windows.other, and no Set-ADUser/Set-ADDomain command line was found in Sysmon process creation. The registry writes under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Authentication on scranton.dmevals.local are LogonUI session bookkeeping (LoggedOnUser DMEVALS\pbeesly, SelectedUserSID, FaceLogon CredProvUncompletedInstances, LogonSoundPlayed) written by C:\windows\system32\LogonUI.exe, plus the standard CredentialEnrollmentManagerUserSvc_13619b service keys written by services.exe — normal interactive-logon behaviour, not MFA tampering.

title: No hybrid-identity / federation or directory-service modification
summary: No 5136 directory-service change events were returned in windows.security or windows.other, and no PowerShell script block containing Connect-MsolService/Connect-AzureAD was found. The only hybrid-identity-adjacent activity is dsregcmd.exe on newyork.dmevals.local loading cryptdll.dll at 03:06:14, which is the standard device-registration client loading the crypto manager DLL.

title: No Network Provider DLL registration
summary: No 4657 write to NetworkProvider/Credential-related registry keys and no PowerShell script block containing NetworkProvider/New-ItemProperty were returned. The registry writes touching credential-related paths on scranton.dmevals.local are MuiCache entries for CredentialEnrollmentManager.exe written by services.exe and the Winlogon PasswordExpiryNotification values written by winlogon.exe — standard OS behaviour, not a network provider DLL registration.

title: No adversary-in-the-middle activity; observed credential theft is PsExec lateral movement with plaintext credentials
summary: Hunting for AiTM positioning (rogue SMB/relay hosts, name-resolution anomalies, network tampering) produced no attacker-in-the-middle evidence in any dataset. The real malicious activity in the Windows window is different: user pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local ran PsExec64.exe from PowerShell four times (03:11:18, 03:12:25, 03:13:28, 03:14:42) against \\NASHUA with the password supplied in cleartext on the command line, staging C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe on nashua.dmevals.local via ADMIN$ (5145 at 03:10:23) and installing PSEXESVC (4697/7045) four times. That is lateral movement / credential misuse, not AiTM. The only 'network' hits were benign: netsh.exe trace start/stop spawned by the Azure NetworkWatcherAgent, and svchost.exe -k LocalServiceNetworkRestricted -p -s Dhcp (the DHCP client service).

title: No LLMNR/NBT-NS poisoning or SMB relay; SMB traffic is normal domain authentication
summary: Name-resolution and SMB activity in the Zeek capture (2020-04-30, non-overlapping with the Windows window) shows only ordinary domain behaviour: wpad.dmevals.local lookups returning NXDOMAIN every ~10 minutes from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6, NetBIOS broadcast lookups for SCRANTON/NASHUA to 10.0.1.255, and LDAP/Kerberos SRV queries against the DC 10.0.0.4. SMB sessions are Kerberos/GSSAPI-authenticated to the DC (10.0.0.4) and to 10.0.1.6, with no unauthenticated relay-style SMB to an unexpected host. No PowerShell script block referenced responder, mitm, llmnr or nbt-ns (zero hits), and no 4657 registry change to DNSClient was recorded. The 4697 service installs in the Windows window are PSEXESVC (lateral movement) and Windows per-user services, not relay tooling.

title: No ARP cache poisoning; MAC/IP pairings are consistent per host
summary: Stacking L2 addresses on Zeek conn records shows three source MACs (00:0d:3a:13:e3:69, 00:0d:3a:4d:42:f2, fc:bd:67:e1:a9:c1) and responder MACs 12:34:56:78:9a:bc plus broadcast ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff. The 12:34:56:78:9a:bc value is a synthetic/placeholder MAC used by the capture environment, not a rogue device claiming multiple IPs. The 00:35:26 flows from 10.0.1.4 to 10.0.1.6 on 445 are recorded by the second sensor (bobs.bigwheel.local) with that sensor's own view of the same hosts, and no single MAC is seen claiming multiple distinct IPs in a way that indicates gratuitous ARP poisoning. No PowerShell script block referenced arp or netsh interface (zero hits), and no netsh interface/ARP manipulation command was executed on any host.

title: No DHCP spoofing; DHCP traffic is the local client service only
summary: No DHCP spoofing indicators exist in the collected data. The windows.other System channel contains no DHCP server/client event codes (1341/1342/1020/1063 returned zero hits), the Zeek capture contains no dhcp log type at all (only conn, files, ssl, x509, dce_rpc, http, dns, kerberos, dpd, smb_files, weird, smb_mapping, notice, pe), and no PowerShell script block mentioned Dhcp. Sysmon network connections show no traffic to UDP 67/68; the only DHCP-related process is the legitimate svchost.exe -k LocalServiceNetworkRestricted -p -s Dhcp client service on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:19:11.

title: Credential theft on scranton: PowerShell full-access LSASS handle plus Kerberos ticket requests for krbtgt
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local a PowerShell process (PID 2976, launched 02:58:44Z as pbeesly from control.exe with '-noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden' and an IEX-decoded payload) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff at 03:05:16Z — full-access handles consistent with credential/ticket extraction. The same session ran discovery, persistence, private-key export, keystroke capture and exfil functions. On newyork.dmevals.local (DC) 4769 events show pbeesly@DMEVALS.LOCAL requesting a krbtgt service ticket at 03:04:04Z and SCRANTON$@DMEVALS.LOCAL requesting krbtgt tickets at 03:19:13Z and 03:19:15Z, all AES256 (0x12) and successful. The zeek capture (non-overlapping window) shows only normal AES256 AS/TGS for pbeesly, so no forged/downgraded tickets are visible there.

title: No golden-ticket evidence: krbtgt TGS requests are AES256 and no forged-ticket indicators
summary: All 28 4769 events on newyork.dmevals.local have TicketEncryptionType 0x12 (AES256) and Status 0x0; the krbtgt service-ticket requests by pbeesly (03:04:04Z) and SCRANTON$ (03:19:13Z, 03:19:15Z) are ordinary TGS requests with no RC4 downgrade, no anomalous principals and no 4672 special-privilege logons attributable to a forged principal (the 4672 aggregation returned no buckets). No golden-ticket forging is observable; the LSASS access is reported under T1558 as credential theft.

title: No silver-ticket indicators in TGS requests
summary: The 4769 service-ticket requests on newyork.dmevals.local are for machine accounts (NEWYORK$, NASHUA$, SCRANTON$, WEC$) and krbtgt, all AES256 (0x12) with Status 0x0 and normal ticket options; no service-account SPN ticket burst or RC4 service ticket typical of silver-ticket use was observed. No PowerShell script block referenced silver tickets or SPNs.

title: No Kerberoasting observed
summary: No PowerShell script block contained Kerberoast/Invoke-Kerberoast/Rubeus strings, and the 4769 stack shows only AES256 tickets for machine accounts and krbtgt — no RC4 (0x17) service-ticket requests for user SPNs that would indicate Kerberoasting. The credential theft on scranton targeted LSASS memory rather than service-ticket roasting.

title: No AS-REP roasting observed
summary: Zeek kerberos records (2020-04-30 window) show only pbeesly AS exchanges to krbtgt/DMEVALS.LOCAL that first return KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED and then succeed with aes256-cts-hmac-sha1-96 — i.e. pre-authentication is enforced, so no AS-REP roasting. No PowerShell script block referenced AS-REP/GetNPUsers/DontRequirePreAuth.

title: Credential theft and certificate/private-key export by PowerShell on SCRANTON (pbeesly) — no forged web credential observed
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly ran an interactive PowerShell session (PID 2976, launched 02:58:44 from control.exe /name Microsoft.BackupAndRestoreCenter with -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden and an IEX-decoded bitmap payload) that performed credential access: at 03:04:56 it defined and ran Get-PrivateKeys, which enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and exports each certificate with a thumbprint to a random .pfx file in the user's Downloads folder (coyn5igj.3io.pfx created 03:04:57); at 03:05:16 the same PowerShell.exe opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1FFFFF (full access, call trace ending in an UNKNOWN module) and again with 0x1f3fff; it then ran screen capture (gwq4xdwv.s5g.bmp, 03:06:00), Get-Clipboard, Get-Keystrokes, and staged an archive at C:\Users\pbeesly\AppData\Roaming\OfficeSupplies.7z (03:08:35) with a cleanup function that deletes *.pfx/*.bmp/*.png and OfficeSupplies.7z. It then moved laterally to NASHUA with Invoke-Command and PsExec64 using the cleartext password for dmevals\pbeesly, producing 4648 explicit-credential logons on scranton (10.0.1.6) and PSEXESVC.exe logons on nashua. The stolen material (exported private keys/certificates, LSASS memory, keystrokes, clipboard) is the raw material for forging web credentials, but no forged cookie or SAML assertion was observed being used: no cookie/SAML/token strings in PowerShell 4104 script blocks, no SAML/ADFS/token URLs in Zeek HTTP, and the only cookie-path file event is a benign svchost INetCookies write. The technique family is therefore assessed as malicious credential access on the host, with the forging step itself not observed.

title: No forged web cookies observed; only cookie-path file event is a benign svchost INetCookies write
summary: The single file-creation event matching a cookie store is svchost.exe writing C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-b484-4973-bbf2-a04208ecd4d4\AC\INetCookies on scranton.dmevals.local at 03:21:05 — a normal LocalService package cache write, not browser cookie theft or injection. No PowerShell 4104 script block in the window contained cookie/Set-Cookie/session strings, and the Zeek HTTP records (2020-04-30, non-overlapping window) show only 10.0.1.4 -> 192.168.0.4 requests with no cookie or session-token evidence retrievable. The credential theft on scranton (LSASS access, keystrokes, clipboard) could enable session hijacking, but no forged cookie was observed.

title: No SAML token forgery observed; certificate/private-key export is the closest precursor
summary: No SAML assertion, NotOnOrAfter or Assertion strings appear in PowerShell 4104 script blocks, no process command line references saml/token/cert, and no Zeek HTTP request targets saml/adfs/token URLs. However, on scranton.dmevals.local the attacker-run PowerShell executed Get-PrivateKeys at 03:04:56, exporting every LocalMachine certificate with a thumbprint to random .pfx files (coyn5igj.3io.pfx at 03:04:57) using the hardcoded password 'saribas' — private keys and certificates are exactly the material used to sign forged SAML tokens, so this is a plausible precursor, but the forging/use of a token itself was not observed in these datasets.

title: No MFA/2FA request-generation activity observed; windows.other hits are routine WMI provider and RSoP events
summary: The only T1621 check with hits (C355, 85 events in windows.other) consists entirely of WMI provider start events (5857, 36 events: dsccore, CIMWin32, deploymentprovider, dnsclientcim, StorageWMI, MSVDS__PROVIDER, Win32_WIN32_TERMINALSERVICE_Prov, WMIProv, BcdProv, SppProvider, all 'result code 0x0' under wmiprvse.exe) and WMI RSoP DeleteInstance events (5858, 49 events, 48 on newyork.dmevals.local with ResultCode 0x80041002 for RSOP_ExtensionStatus GUIDs). The single 5858 on scranton.dmevals.local is a WMI ExecNotificationQuery for Win32_ProcessStartTrace WHERE ProcessName = 'wsmprovhost.exe' (ResultCode 0x80041032). None of these are authentication or MFA-push events; they are normal WMI/RSoP housekeeping. No 4625 failures exist in windows.security (C352/C353 zero hits), no MFA/2FA/authenticator strings in PowerShell 4104 script blocks (C354 zero; the one 'verify' match is a PowerShellGet resource-string block on scranton under user pbeesly), no login/auth/mfa command lines in Sysmon process creation (C356 zero), and no login/auth/mfa HTTP URLs in zeek (C357 zero). The only authentication activity of note is a single NTLM network logon (4624 type 3, NtLmSsp, NTLM V2, workstation 10.0.1.4, source 172.18.39.2) for pbeesly on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-02T03:20:41Z followed by a type 10 RemoteInteractive logon for the same account at 03:20:46Z — a successful logon sequence, not repeated MFA prompts or push bombing. At 2020-05-02T03:04:57.460Z Sysmon recorded the resulting file C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\coyn5igj.3io.pfx created by powershell.exe (PID 3876), and at 03:04:57.272-03:04:57.428Z the same powershell.exe (PID 3876) wrote certificate store blobs under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\Remote Desktop\Certificates\615B93C2D2B647D1670500B3338EAAEC83BA5646\Blob and HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\SystemCertificates\MY\Certificates\48B5E43D09D080DF8863152FD22ED7C43443D499\Blob. This is theft of authentication certificates (including private keys) for later use/forgery. The other certificate-store registry writes in the window (lsass.exe, svchost.exe, smss.exe, taskhostw.exe, and the single 4657 on nashua.dmevals.local by NASHUA$ via C:\Windows\Sysmon.exe) are routine OS certificate-store maintenance and are not attacker activity.

title: Routine certificate-store registry writes and Kerberos TGT requests (benign context)
summary: The remaining T1649 check hits are normal system behaviour. The other SystemCertificates registry writes in sysmon came from lsass.exe, svchost.exe, smss.exe and taskhostw.exe (AuthRoot, Windows Live ID Token Issuer, ACRS physical-store values) — standard Windows certificate propagation. The 14 Kerberos 4768 TGT requests on newyork.dmevals.local were for pbeesly (9) and the SCRANTON$ machine account (5) from internal addresses 10.0.1.4/10.0.1.6, with no PKINIT/certificate-based anomalies visible. The Zeek x509 subjects (rempel.group.net 376, conn.sons.info 2) are from a non-overlapping 2020-04-30 window and show no forged-certificate indicators. Note: the malicious certificate export itself is reported in the separate malicious finding.
